                                            PROJECT NO. 58481

 RULEMAKING TO IMPLEMENT                                  §         PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
 LARGE LOAD INTERCONNECTION                               §
 STANDARDS UNDER PURA § 37.0561                           §                        OF TEXAS

                                       COMMENTS OF
                             TEXAS ELECTRIC COOPERATIVES, INC.

        Texas Electric Cooperatives, Inc. (TEC) respectfully submits these comments in response

to the discussion draft proposed by the Public Utility Commission of Texas Staff (Staff) regarding

large load interconnection standards.1 TEC is the statewide association of electric cooperatives

operating in Texas, representing its members except as their interests may be separately

represented.2 The discussion draft directed responses to be filed by December 19, 2025. These

comments are timely filed.

                                           I.       Staff Questions

1.      Should the commission define parameters for determining whether a large load
        customer is pursuing a substantially similar interconnection request? If so, how
        should the commission define those parameters?

        TEC recognizes the importance of addressing potentially duplicative interconnection

requests and the impact that such requests may have on future load projections that drive important

decisions with significant cost impacts, such as transmission needs and the planning reserve

requirement. The Commission should define clear parameters for determining whether a large load

customer is pursuing one or more duplicative interconnection requests, whether the duplicative

interconnection request(s) are being pursued in more than one utility service territory and in which

service territories such interconnection requests are being considered.


        1
            Discussion Draft w/12.19 Comment Deadline (Dec. 1, 2025) (“Discussion Draft”).
        2
            TEC’s 76 members include distribution cooperatives that provide retail electric utility service to
approximately 5,000,000 consumers in statutorily authorized service areas that encompass more than half of the total
area of the state. TEC’s G&T members generally acquire generation resources and power supply for their member
distribution cooperatives and deliver electricity to them at wholesale.



                                                                                                                  1
        TEC suggests that the focus of the parameters should not be limited to how similar two

proposals are, but rather an analysis of the resulting status impact of the approval of one proposal

on another. For example: a company may submit two large load data center proposals that differ

in their megawatt (MW) requirements, site layout, or whether the proposed data center will utilize

backup generation. While the proposals are not substantially similar, the company may intend to

proceed with only one of the two projects. The projects are not substantially similar, but the

approval of one project will directly impact whether the company intends to proceed with the

second project proposal.

       TEC suggests that the more appropriate framing of the inquiry during the large load

interconnection process is not whether multiple proposals are similar to one another but rather if

the approval of one proposal will have a direct impact on the viability of another proposal. A sworn

affidavit from the highest-ranking officer of the company that identifies all other locations in Texas

that may be pursued if the location at issue does not proceed could be utilized. Similarity between

proposals may be a factor in the analysis but should not be the sole or determinative consideration.

This approach ensures that the Commission’s rules capture the practical realities of project

development while avoiding unnecessary duplication in interconnection requests.

2.     Proposed subsections (c)(3), (e)(3), and (h)(3) require the disclosure of specific
       information related to a substantially similar request for interconnection and allows
       a large load customer to anonymize competitively sensitive details. Should the
       Commission list what is and is not competitively sensitive (e.g., load zone is not
       competitively sensitive information)? If so, what information should and should not
       be considered competitively sensitive such that the interconnecting utility and
       ERCOT can identify whether there is a duplicate request, or a request is unlikely to
       materialize?

       TEC recommends that the Commission give deference to the interconnecting entity, in

consultation with the large load customer, in determining what information should be considered

competitively sensitive. This approach ensures that those most directly involved in the



                                                                                                    2
 interconnection process can appropriately safeguard information that, if disclosed, could affect

market position or project viability.

       TEC is not opposed to the Commission identifying certain categories of information that

are definitively not competitively sensitive, such as load zone, and listing those items explicitly in

the proposed rule. Doing so would provide clarity while still preserving flexibility for

interconnecting entities and customers to protect information that legitimately warrants

confidentiality.

3.     Should the commission require a large load customer to notify the interconnecting
       electric utility and ERCOT of any change to information that is initially disclosed in
       response to this rule or only material changes to the information disclosed? If only
       material changes, how should “material change” be defined?

       TEC understands that information may change often throughout the development of a large

load project. Immediate disclosure of immaterial changes is not necessary and, in fact, can be

counterproductive. TEC recommends that material information, information that could impact

decision making or analysis by the interconnecting electric provider or ERCOT, should be

disclosed immediately. Immaterial or minor changes may be updated throughout the course of the

project development on an as needed basis. TEC recommends that rather than leaving the decision

to the load as to what is material or immaterial, that the Commission state that any information

that may change the size, scope, location, or interconnection point of the project, or the timelines

associated with the progress of the project, be considered material.

       ERCOT Planning Guide Section 9, Modifications of Large Load Project Information,

already provides a definition of “material changes” and could serve as an appropriate reference

point for the Commission in drafting this requirement. Aligning the rule with existing ERCOT

guidance would ensure consistency, reduce unnecessary administrative burden, and focus

disclosure obligations on information that truly matters for system planning and reliability.



                                                                                                    3
 4.       Proposed subsection (k)(1) authorizes an interconnecting electric utility to refund
         20% of a large load customer’s security after energization and ratably as the large
         load customer meets the milestones identified in the customer’s schedule for phased
         energization of its contracted load. Should the commission standardize the rate for
         refund for reaching milestones identified in the customer’s schedule for phased
         energization (e.g., 20% for each year of operations until the full amount of security is
         refunded)? If so, how should the commission standardize the refund?

         TEC opposes the standardization of refund amounts and processes in the proposed rule;

however, the Commission should explicitly state what types of costs are to be directly assigned to

the large load and what security is required with respect to those items, including the length of

time security is to be held. The interconnecting entity should have the right and the obligation to

hold security until such time as the costs incurred by the large load are no longer at risk of not

being paid and consequently increasing TCOS. Any security should be liquid, but the form of

security should be determined by the interconnecting entity.

5.       Are changes to the commission’s other substantive rules necessary to align with this
         rulemaking? If so, what changes need to be made to which rules?

         No comments at this time.

                                                 II.      Comments

A.       Use of the term “Interconnecting Electric Utility”

         The term “interconnecting electric utility” is used throughout the proposed rule language

as a set defined term specific to the proposed rule.3 However, throughout the Commission’s rules,

the term “electric utility” is generally not applied to electric cooperatives and municipally owned

utilities.4




         3
             Discussion Draft at 5, proposed § 25.194(b)(5).
         4
             16 Texas Administrative Code (TAC) § 25.5(42)(G).



                                                                                                 4
            TEC does not dispute that certain sections of Senate Bill 6 are applicable to electric

cooperatives and understands that the use of a single term will ease the drafting burden on

Commission Staff. Rather, TEC is concerned that use of the term “interconnecting electric utility”

could cause unintended confusion regarding the rule’s applicability and conflicting definitions due

to the statutory distinction between electric cooperatives, municipally owned utilities, and “electric

utilities”. As an alternative to “interconnecting electric utility”, TEC recommends using the term

“interconnecting utility” which would be defined to include “an electric utility, electric cooperative

or municipally-owned utility interconnecting a large load, and if different from the interconnecting

utility, the entity with the right and obligation to provide service to the load pursuant to a certificate

of convenience and necessity approved by the Commission.” The change would begin in the first

subsection of the rule, §25.194(a). The interconnecting utility term can be used and would only

require a search and replace throughout the rule, but use of different terminology will ensure

clarity.

B.         Study Fees

           TEC appreciates Staff’s recognition of the need for large load consumers to pay the fees

associated with their interconnection studies. Section 25.194(c)(7) as proposed requires the load

pay a study fee of not less than $114,000 or $314,000, depending on the MW size of the load. The

proposed rule also requires that the large load pay the full study fee if it exceeds those amounts.

TEC agrees that there should be a standard framework for study fee minimums such that both

loads and utilities share the same expectations with respect to studies.5 However, the required

study fee minimum should stay at the statutory level of $100,000 with the large load required to




           5
               Discussion Draft at 8 – 9, proposed § 25.194(c)(7).



                                                                                                        5
 pay the full study amount for any study that exceeds the minimum.6 The vast majority of studies

will exceed this minimum, and the inability to pay the minimum amounts for the studies, given the

comparison to the expenditures being made to serve the load, would indicate that a load is not

serious.

       TEC members noted that requiring minimum study amounts in excess of the $100,000 in

statute increases the likelihood that the interconnecting utility will need to carry excess cash on

hand for a potential refund, increasing administrative complexity. The use of the statutory

minimum also obviates the need to continuously revisit set minimums given that the loads will be

responsible for all study costs in excess of the $100,000 minimum in statute. TEC therefore

recommends deleting §25.194(c)(7)(B), since if the study exceeds the $100,000 under

§25.194(c)(7)(A), the load will be required to pay the full amount.

C.     Additional Study Fees for Increases in Requested or Contracted Peak Demand

       Proposed subsection (d)(2) requires a large load customer to pay any required increase in

the interconnection study fee associated with an increase in the requested or contracted peak

demand.7 TEC believes that this should be expanded to include all study fees not just increased

interconnection study fees. For example, if a restudy is required, that cost should be the

responsibility of the large load. TEC supports the requirement that the large load pay any required

increase in study fees but would appreciate clarification regarding notice to the large load

customer. In particular, in a scenario where the interconnecting utility does not require an

additional study fee, but ERCOT or another TSP does require an additional fee, will it be

incumbent upon ERCOT to seek the additional fee from the large load consumer? Or will the



       6
           PURA § 37.0561(f).
       7
           Discussion Draft at 10, proposed § 25.194(d)(2).



                                                                                                 6
 interconnecting utility be required to act as an intermediary and pass along the additional fee

requirements? TEC appreciates any clarification.

D.     Financial Security on a Dollar per MW Basis

       Proposed subsection (e)(8) requires a large load customer to pay financial security to the

interconnecting entity in the amount of $50,000 per MW of contracted peak demand. TEC does

not have a position on whether this amount is sufficient to ensure a large load customer has made

satisfactory proof of financial commitment. TEC intends to provide input on this value as we gather

additional information from our member systems.

E.     Notification of Additional Study Requirements

       The proposed rule language contemplates the need for the interconnecting utility to act as

a middleman between ERCOT and the large load when ERCOT seeks an additional study.8 TEC

certainly understands the potential need for further study and does not object to further required

study, and believes that the interconnecting utility should remain involved in the information flow;

however, it may be more efficient and avoid unnecessary delays if, since ERCOT would have the

large load’s information, ERCOT provided notice directly to the large load and copied the

interconnecting utility on the notification, rather than relying on the interconnecting utility to act

as a middleman for notification purposes.

F.     Contribution in Aid of Construction (CIAC)

       Proposed subsection (h)(9) purports to use CIAC as the preferred form of passing costs

along to large load consumers.9 Proposed (h)(9) also uses the term “interconnecting electric

utility”, which the proposal previously defines as including electric cooperatives and municipally




       8
           Discussion Draft at 15, proposed § 25.194(g).
       9
           Discussion Draft at 20 – 21, proposed § 25.194(h)(9).



                                                                                                    7
 owned utilities (MOUs), unless the rule is amended as recommended by TEC to avoid confusion.10

Thus, as written, the proposed rule would require electric cooperatives and MOUs to use CIAC as

the sole method for passing costs along to large load consumers. This runs counter to statue, which

states:

          An electric cooperative or municipally owned utility that has not adopted customer
          choice shall pass through to a large load customer who is subject to the standards
          adopted under Section 37.0561 the reasonable costs to interconnect the large load
          in a manner determined by the electric cooperative or municipally owned utility.11

          The statute gives electric cooperatives and MOUs the exclusive right to determine how to

pass through costs to a large load consumer. Many may very well use CIAC, but that is not a

determination to be made in this rule. Rather, that determination is reserved to the local governing

body of the electric cooperative or MOU.12 TEC recommends specifying that subsection (h)(9)

only applies to investor-owned utilities and MOUs and electric cooperatives that choose to utilize

subsection (h)(9) at the local level. Otherwise, MOUs and electric cooperatives shall determine

their own methodology for passing costs to the large load consumer in accordance with PURA

§35.004 (c-2).

                                                  III.     Conclusion

          TEC appreciates the opportunity to provide comments in response to the discussion draft

and looks forward to working with the Commission and other stakeholders on this project.




          10
               Discussion Draft at 5, proposed § 25.194(b)(5).
          11
               Public Utility Regulatory Act (PURA) § 35.004(c-2) (emphasis added).
          12
               Id.

                                      PROJECT NO. 58481

 RULEMAKING TO IMPLEMENT                         §        PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
 LARGE LOAD INTERCONNECTION                      §
 STANDARDS UNDER PURA § 37.0561                  §                     OF TEXAS


                  Executive Summary of Texas Electric Cooperatives, Inc.

Texas Electric Cooperatives, Inc. makes the following recommendations:

1)     TEC suggests that the more appropriate question to ask during the large load
       interconnection process is not whether multiple proposals are similar to one another, but
       rather if the approval of one proposal will have a direct impact on the status of another
       proposal.

2)     TEC recommends that the Commission give deference to the interconnecting facility owner
       as to what they consider to be competitively sensitive information.

3)     TEC recommends that only material information, information that could impact the
       decision making or analysis of the interconnecting electric provider or ERCOT, should be
       disclosed immediately. Immaterial or minor changes may be updated throughout the course
       of the project development on an as needed basis.

4)     TEC opposes the standardization of refund amounts and processes. The amount of a refund
       or the appropriateness of a refund at all is best determined by the interconnecting electric
       provider.

5)     As an alternative to “interconnecting electric utility”, TEC recommends using the term
       “interconnecting utility”.

6)     TEC believes it makes more sense to remove the set study fee dollar amounts and simply
       require the large load to pay the required study fees in excess of the $100,000 statutory
       minimum from the interconnecting utility and ERCOT.

7)     TEC supports the requirement for additional study fees as needed but would appreciate
       clarification regarding notice to the large load customer, whether it will be the
       interconnecting utility or ERCOT?

8)     TEC understands the potential need for further study and does not object to further required
       study, but it may be more efficient, since ERCOT would have the large load consumer’s
       information, if ERCOT sent notification directly to the large load consumer.

9)     TEC recommends specifying that subsection (h)(9) only applies to the investor-owned
       utilities and MOUs and electric cooperatives that choose to utilize (h)(9).

                                      PROJECT NO. 58481

 RULEMAKING TO IMPLEMENT                          §        PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
 LARGE LOAD INTERCONNECTION                       §
 STANDARDS UNDER PURA § 37.0561                   §                     OF TEXAS


                  Executive Summary of Texas Electric Cooperatives, Inc.

Texas Electric Cooperatives, Inc. makes the following recommendations:

1)     TEC suggests that the more appropriate question to ask during the large load
       interconnection process is not whether multiple proposals are similar to one another, but
       rather if the approval of one proposal will have a direct impact on the status of another
       proposal.

2)     TEC recommends that the Commission give deference to the interconnecting facility owner
       as to what they consider to be competitively sensitive information.

3)     TEC recommends that only material information, information that could impact the
       decision making or analysis of the interconnecting electric provider or ERCOT, should be
       disclosed immediately. Immaterial or minor changes may be updated throughout the course
       of the project development on an as needed basis.

4)     TEC opposes the standardization of refund amounts and processes. The amount of a refund
       or the appropriateness of a refund at all is best determined by the interconnecting electric
       provider.

5)     As an alternative to "interconnecting electric utility", TEC recommends using the term
       "interconnecting utility".

6)     TEC believes it makes more sense to remove the set study fee dollar amounts and simply
       require the large load to pay the required study fees in excess of the $100,000 statutory
       minimum from the interconnecting utility and ERCOT.

7)     TEC supports the requirement for additional study fees as needed but would appreciate
       clarification regarding notice to the large load customer, whether it will be the
       interconnecting utility or ERCOT?

8)     TEC understands the potential need for further study and does not obj ect to further required
       study, but it may be more efficient, since ERCOT would have the large load consumer' s
       information, if ERCOT sent notification directly to the large load consumer.

9)     TEC recommends specifying that subsection (h)(9) only applies to the investor-owned
       utilities and MOUs and electric cooperatives that choose to utilize (h)(9).
